scenes.heading: Data Vault Modeling
scenes.narration: Data Vault is a modeling method built for agility and auditability, decomposing the warehouse into hubs, links, and satellites that absorb change without rework.

scenes.heading: The three building blocks
bullets: Everything is insert-only and fully audited
scenes.narration: Hubs store the distinct business keys of core concepts like customer or product, decoupled from any descriptive detail. Links capture the relationships and transactions between hubs, such as which customer placed which order. Satellites hang off hubs and links to hold the descriptive attributes that change over time, keeping full history. Crucially the entire model is insert-only and load-time stamped, so it is inherently auditable and never loses history.

scenes.heading: Data Vault vs dimensional star schema
scenes.narration: Data Vault is highly agile: adding a new source or attribute means adding a satellite or link without reworking existing structures, and its insert-only design gives complete auditability. However it is not friendly to query directly because reconstructing a business view requires many joins. A dimensional star schema is simple and fast for BI tools to query, but it often needs rework when source structures change. The common pattern is to load raw data into a Data Vault, then build star schemas on top for consumption.

scenes.heading: Loading a Data Vault
steps: Build marts on top for BI
scenes.narration: Loading follows a repeatable pattern. First, business keys are extracted and inserted into hubs, deduplicated so each key appears once. Next, the relationships between those keys are recorded as rows in link tables. Then descriptive attributes are written into satellites, each stamped with its load time. Because loads are insert-only, a changed attribute simply becomes a new satellite row and history is preserved. Finally, query-friendly marts or star schemas are built on top for reporting.

scenes.heading: Why the split into three parts
bullets: Links absorb new relationships without rework
Satellites absorb new or changed attributes
scenes.narration: The three-part split is what gives Data Vault its agility. Hubs isolate the stable business keys that rarely change. Links let you add a brand-new relationship simply by creating a new link table, without touching existing structures. Satellites let you add new attributes or new sources by creating a new satellite, again without rework. And because hubs, links, and satellites are loaded independently, loads can run in parallel without blocking each other, which suits large, evolving warehouses.

scenes.heading: When to choose Data Vault
scenes.narration: Data Vault earns its complexity in specific situations. It fits when you integrate many source systems that change frequently, because it absorbs that churn gracefully. It fits when auditability and full history are hard requirements, as in regulated industries. It suits long-lived enterprise warehouses expected to evolve for years. But it demands a team comfortable with its extra modeling overhead, so for a small, stable warehouse a simpler dimensional model is often the better choice.

scenes.text: Model raw history in an auditable, insert-only vault, then serve query-friendly marts on top for the best of agility and usability.
scenes.narration: Capture raw history in an agile, insert-only Data Vault that absorbs source change and stays fully auditable, then build query-friendly marts on top of it, combining long-term adaptability with day-to-day usability.
